title: Stack versus heap layout
hook: The stack is storage for activation records. The managed heap is where the GC tracks objects. ‘Struct versus class’ is about layout, not a promise that a struct never touches the heap.

sections.heading: What actually lives where
sections.prose: Each thread has a stack. Locals and parameters that are value types sit in that frame or in registers, until something promotes them: boxing, a closure, an async state machine, or a field of a heap object. Reference-type locals are pointers (or managed references) on the stack pointing at objects on the managed heap. The CLR heap is a contiguous reserved region per process; bump allocation for small objects is a pointer increment, which is why gen-0 allocation is cheap compared with malloc. You never pin physical RAM yourself; you work in virtual address space. An async method that awaits Redis will hoist locals the compiler considers live across the await onto the state-machine object — that object is a heap allocation even if the locals were ints.

snippets.label: Same bytes, three homes
snippets.explanation: OnStack can stay in the frame. Boxed copies onto the heap. AcrossAwaitAsync stores stamp on the compiler-generated state machine.

sections.heading: Why interviews mix this with GC
sections.prose: GC only walks the heap. Stack slots are roots: if a local still references a large CSV buffer, that buffer is live. After the local dies, the next gen-0 collection can reclaim it. Pinning (fixed, GCHandleType.Pinned, some interop) prevents compacting around that object; SkiaSharp and other native interop may pin briefly. Prefer stackalloc or Span for short-lived bytes when the APIs allow — that is module 17 territory, but the layout rule starts here: if it is a reference, the object is on the heap until no root can reach it.

interviewTakeaways: Value types are inline; they are on the stack only when their container is a stack frame.
Async, lambdas, and boxing are the usual reasons a ‘stack struct’ becomes a heap field.
Stack slots are GC roots for whatever they still reference.
commonPitfalls: Saying structs never go on the heap.
Keeping a large byte[] in a field of a long-lived singleton ‘for convenience.’
Ignoring that await extends the lifetime of locals to the state machine.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JS numbers are not C# value types. Objects and closures always live in the JS heap. There is no programmer-controlled stack struct for a record of two ints.
